source.title: Mixture of Wide Experts: Sparse Routing for Interpretable Native Coordinates
source.authors: Tavish Mankash; Vardhaman Kalloli; Keshava Prasad; Deepan Muthirayan

record.file_problem: none noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares architectures and evaluates native-coordinate readability using automated descriptions and specificity scores. This is a different measurement from counting polysemantic neurons, but it tests whether architecture and evaluation choices affect how interpretable model coordinates appear.
record.gate_note: The study does not count the share of neurons that respond to unrelated inputs. Its main language-model evidence is a judge-based score on sampled, highly activating contexts; it also reports raw purity, shuffled-description-adjusted specificity, and random-rotation comparisons. The controlled-task localization chart is figure-only. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study compares dense, standard-MoE and MoWE language models on judge-scored readability of native FFN-update coordinates, with loss alongside. This bears on V5: architecture changes how mixed units are, at a stated performance cost. Raw purity and shuffle-corrected specificity rank the models differently, which bears on V7's scoring part. The measured units are FFN output coordinates, not MLP hidden neurons. In dense and standard MoE these coordinates have no privileged basis.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add that the authors conclude sparse routing alone does not make readable coordinates: standard-MoE native coordinates are no more specific than a random rotation. The gain is attributed to disjoint expert outputs. Standard MoE has the best loss, and MoWE beats dense.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces an architectural constraint on expert output coordinates and evaluates readability with judge-written descriptions, shuffled-description correction, and random rotations; it does not reproduce the original neuron-inspection method. It also compares against a post-hoc TopK SAE.
record.method_sensitivity: Readability differs by architecture and representation basis. MoWE is higher than dense in 18 of 19 layers; the reported score also differs between raw purity and shuffled-adjusted specificity. The study does not vary judges or systematically vary activation-range cutoffs.

fits_no_version.finding: A site-matched TopK SAE raises dense specificity by 0.114 but MoWE by only 0.032. This suggests post-hoc dictionaries add less when native units are already specific.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-hoc sparse dictionaries recover more interpretable structure from bases whose native units are more mixed.

record.problems: The all-layer interpretability evaluation uses one checkpoint per architecture, while the loss comparison has two runs per architecture. The evaluation samples 100 live coordinates per layer and relies on an automated language-model judge; the authors note that human ratings and behavioral feature tests would strengthen it. Several controlled-task localization values appear only in a figure. The study does not estimate the fraction of all neurons that are polysemantic.
record.rows_left_out: No further claim-relevant results omitted. Performance, router, throughput, and intervention results not measuring coordinate readability or the architecture/readability tradeoff were not cataloged as separate rows.

untested.parts: There is no count of polysemantic MLP hidden neurons in standard LMs. Measured units are FFN output coordinates, not neurons.
Superposition is discussed but not tested as a cause.
Initialization, regularization and noise without capacity pressure are not tested.
Activation-function changes such as SoLU, convnets and regularization are not tested. No share of polysemantic hidden neurons is reported.
No reinterpretation of canonical polysemantic neurons.
Activation-range dependence is not tested: only top contexts are used. Only one judge is used.

missing.what: Pilot loss: dense best CE 2.8914 versus MoWE 2.9611, so MoWE is worse by 0.07 nats at 10 layers
512-scale loss: standard MoE 4.0331, MoWE 4.1186, dense 4.1524; and fraction of coordinates above 0.7 raw purity, MoE 0.04 versus dense 0.22
Toy task predictive performance is matched: identical bit and exact accuracy, BCE range 0.0008
Code-context share explains the high shuffled floors: MoE native 56.2% code, MoWE rotated 60.1%

record.verdict_notes: Measured units are FFN output (residual-update) coordinates. In dense and standard MoE these have no privileged basis, as dense native equals rotation, so they are not analogous to MLP hidden neurons. In MoWE each coordinate is one expert's scalar output, which is neuron-like. Toy residual-coordinate mixing likewise reflects basis alignment, not V4 polysemanticity without capacity pressure. The specificity audit uses a single checkpoint and a single judge (GPT-5.6 Luna).

versions.untested_parts: No image classifiers or InceptionV1 neurons are tested.
The study evaluates descriptions of sampled language-model FFN-update coordinates, not the share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts.
The study discusses superposition but does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than there are neurons.
No test of initialization, regularization, or training noise producing polysemanticity without capacity pressure.

The study tests dense, standard-MoE, and MoWE architectures and reports predictive performance, but does not test activation-function changes, modern convnets, or the prevalence of polysemantic neurons as a proportion of all neurons.
The study does not establish that canonical mixed-response neurons generally detect one shared feature or related offshoots; its selected case studies do not estimate how often that occurs.
The study compares raw purity with shuffled-description-adjusted specificity and evaluates random rotations. It does not compare alternative judges or systematically vary activation-range cutoffs.

relationships.condition: 19-layer final models (10B tokens), and the toy known-cause task (1,800 steps)
relationships.reason: MoWE native specificity is 0.523 versus dense 0.375, with equal or better loss (2.417 vs 2.452) (r1, r2, r14, r15). Toy localization is better at matched accuracy (r23-r25). Standard MoE is less specific than dense at both scales (r3, r22).
relationships.display_finding: MoWE reached native specificity 0.523 versus 0.375 for dense at equal or better loss (2.417 vs 2.452) and localized the toy known cause better at matched accuracy, while standard MoE was less specific than dense at both scales.

relationships.condition: Comparison with the routing-matched standard MoE, and the shorter 10-layer pilot
relationships.reason: The more readable MoWE costs 0.197 nats of evaluation CE versus standard MoE (r14, r16). In the pilot, dense beats MoWE by 0.07 nats (from the text; not in the rows). Dense output coordinates are no more readable than a random rotation (r4), so part of the gain is a privileged basis rather than fewer polysemantic neurons.
relationships.display_finding: MoWE had 0.197 nats higher evaluation cross-entropy than standard MoE, dense beat MoWE by 0.07 nats in the 10-layer pilot, and dense output coordinates were no more readable than a random rotation, so part of the gain reflects a privileged basis rather than fewer polysemantic neurons.

statements.problem: 0.197 = 2.417 - 2.220 (evaluation CE) is right. The unspecified pilot gap (0.0697) is best logged training CE (2.8914 vs 2.9611), not evaluation CE.
Dense native 0.375 equals its rotation 0.375. MoWE's rotation scores 0.384 vs native 0.523, which supports the basis point.
Only router balance/z-loss are varied (screening, toy sweeps). Dropout, weight decay and L1 are fixed, not varied.
Pilot purities come from the 10-layer pilot (layer 6, 500 coordinates), using an earlier diagnostic the authors say not to compare with final specificity.

statements.correction: Raw purity: MoE 0.630 > MoWE 0.601 > dense 0.573. Specificity: MoWE 0.523 > dense 0.375 > MoE 0.268. MoE goes from first to last; MoWE > dense under both.
statements.problem: 'Reverse the ordering' overstates it. The ranking is reordered, not reversed: MoWE stays above dense under both scores.
